rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Shorten the gradient by one grid step to bring the last peak below 10 minutes. Holding the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed tests whether the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5 under modest compression.

Restore the gradient duration that fully resolved the mixture and raise temperature one step to shorten retention. This tests whether temperature can bring the last peak below 10 minutes while preserving or improving the critical separation.
The critical pair converges as temperature rises, suggesting a selectivity crossover. Test 55 °C to seek separation on the other side of that crossover while bringing the last peak below 10 minutes.

After the temperature-induced crossover, a steeper gradient may now widen the critical pair rather than compress it. Shortening to 14 minutes tests this while reducing run time; the other pairs currently have resolution margin.

Shortening the gradient improved the critical pair from R 1.38 to 1.47; another two-minute reduction may bring it above 1.5. The next-tightest pair has R 2.18, leaving some margin for compression while targeting CRF 1.0.
Injection 6 attained the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark and test whether a shorter gradient preserves full resolution. The pair currently at R 1.59 is likely to limit further compression.

Shift and narrow the solvent window while restoring the gradient slope of the fully resolved injection 6. This may shorten retention without the resolution loss caused by steepening alone; the first peak should remain retained and the last should elute within the gradient.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the pair at R 1.12 while retaining the shifted starting composition. This may recover full resolution with a last peak earlier than injection 6; the other critical pair currently has R 1.61.

Keep injection 6 as the maximum-score benchmark and explore a faster, higher-temperature regime. The combination may move the limiting middle pair through its selectivity crossover and restore separation in reversed order, while improving the other temperature-sensitive pair.

The limiting pair appears to have crossed elution order at 60 °C; further steepening may now increase its separation. Test a six-minute gradient while monitoring the neighboring pair at R 2.14 for compression, retaining injection 6 as the proven maximum-score method.

The faster high-temperature regime compromises multiple middle pairs, so test the opposite temperature limit for a different selectivity pattern. A ten-minute broad gradient should keep all compounds observable and may provide a faster fully resolved alternative to injection 6.

Return to the promising narrowed-window series: lowering phi1 another step should raise the limiting pair from R 1.32 to approximately 1.5 while preserving the other critical separation. This targets a second maximum-score method with all peaks comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction at 60 °C separates the limiting middle pair beyond its crossover without excessive gradient compression. This explores a faster alternative to injection 6, while checking that the early peaks remain sufficiently retained and resolved.

Return to 55 °C and narrow the gradient further to seek more resolution margin than the two proven maximum-score methods. The higher starting fraction should shorten early retention, while the shallower slope should help the limiting middle pair and keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Refine the fully resolved injection 13 by lowering phi1 one step, aiming to increase its minimum resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. The observed slope response suggests the two critical pairs should remain above R 1.5.

Flatten injection 15 by one solvent-endpoint step to lift its limiting R 1.41 pair above 1.5, while its other critical pair has R 1.74. This targets a maximum-score method with greater resolution margin, provided the last peak remains below 10 minutes.

Test a modest temperature reduction from injection 2 to improve its temperature-sensitive critical pair without lengthening the gradient. This explores an alternative fully resolved selectivity regime, while retaining injection 6 as the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Lower the starting organic fraction relative to injection 14 to recover early-pair retention, while steepening the gradient to seek separation beyond the middle-pair crossover. This tests a faster alternative, with injection 6 retained as the proven maximum-score benchmark.

Trim injection 6’s unused high-organic tail while preserving its starting composition and gradient slope exactly. The last peak previously exited near phi 0.57, so this method should retain full resolution and CRF 1.0 with a lower final organic fraction.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 17, from 0.045 to 0.0464 organic fraction per minute, to shorten retention while using its resolution margin. Both critical pairs should remain above R 1.5, targeting a slightly faster version of that fully resolved method.

Test a gradient slope between the fully resolved injection 6 and the faster injection 7 to refine the shortest-resolution boundary. The pair at R 1.59 in injection 6 is at risk, so retain injection 6 as the proven maximum-score method.
